program_overview.title: Informatik Companion, Klasse 5 to 10 (in English)
program_overview.tagline: School Informatik explained slowly and clearly, live and in English: your mentor matches your pace and accent, so every class is subject help and English practice at once.
program_overview.description:
This is a live online course for pupils in Germany in Klasse 5 to 10 who have Informatik at school, or will soon, and want a patient teacher beside them. It covers what school Informatik covers: algorithms first in Scratch and then in Python, information and data, how computers and networks work, and how informatics changes everyday life, including AI. Classes are live and taught in English only. The mentor matches the pupil's pace and accent: speaks clearly, slows down, rephrases and checks understanding, so a pupil whose first language is German gets Informatik help and steady spoken English practice in the same hour. We never teach in German, but our materials put the German school term beside the English one (Algorithmus and algorithm, Struktogramm and structure chart, EVA-Prinzip and input, process, output) so pupils can link class to their school notes.

Informatik looks very different from one Land to the next. The Gesellschaft für Informatik (GI) Informatik-Monitor 2026/27 reports that NRW teaches "das Pflichtfach Informatik in den Jahrgangsstufen 5 und 6" at all general school types, Niedersachsen has had compulsory Informatik in Klasse 9 and 10 since 2024/25, Hamburg has required four weekly hours since 2025/26 (spread over Klasse 7 to 10), Sachsen teaches it one hour a week in Klasse 7 to 10, and Baden-Württemberg introduced the compulsory subject Informatik und Medienbildung from 2025/26, starting in Klasse 5 and 6. The same monitor names six Länder with no Informatik that is compulsory for everyone: Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Hessen, Rheinland-Pfalz and Sachsen-Anhalt. Bremen plans a compulsory subject from 2027/28 and Rheinland-Pfalz from 2028/29.

So the course is built on the common ground: the five content areas of the GI's recommended education standards for Sekundarstufe I (Information und Daten, Algorithmen, Sprachen und Automaten, Informatiksysteme, and Informatik, Mensch und Gesellschaft). In the first class we ask which Land, school type and Klasse the pupil is in and what the class is doing now, and the mentor weights the course toward that. Every exercise is our own. We are an independent online school with teachers in India; we are not a German school, we are not linked to any Land ministry or to the GI, and we do not issue German grades or qualifications.
what_makes_this_different: Live classes in English only, with a mentor who matches the pupil's pace and accent: clear speech, slower explanations, rephrasing and frequent checks
Subject help and English practice in the same hour: pupils explain their own programs out loud in English every class
Organised around the five content areas of the GI recommended standards for Sekundarstufe I, the common ground under every Land's Informatik
Weighted to the pupil's own Land and Klasse after the first class, because Informatik differs so much between NRW, Bayern, Sachsen, Hamburg and the rest
Scratch first for younger pupils, then a careful move to Python, so nobody meets text code before the ideas make sense
German school terms printed beside the English ones in our notes, so class links straight back to the school exercise book

learning_path.phase_1: Algorithmen and Information und Daten with Scratch: sequences, loops, conditions, variables, binary and encoding, structure charts and puzzle-style thinking
learning_path.phase_2: From blocks to Python: variables, conditions, loops, functions, lists and strings, simple encryption and working with data tables
learning_path.phase_3: Informatiksysteme, networks, Sprachen und Automaten, and Informatik, Mensch und Gesellschaft including AI, with school-test style review and a final project

career_outcomes: Confidence in school Informatik lessons and tests from Klasse 5 to 10
Writing, reading and fixing short programs in Scratch and Python
Explaining an algorithm clearly, with a structure chart or in words
Understanding how data is stored, sent across a network and protected
Thinking critically about AI, privacy and online safety
More fluent, more confident spoken English about technical topics

phase_1_algorithms_and_data_with_scratch.title: PHASE 1: Algorithmen and Information und Daten with Scratch (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_algorithms_and_data_with_scratch.description: The two GI content areas every Land starts with, taught visually in Scratch so the ideas come before the syntax.

month_1_starting_points.title: Month 1: Starting Points, Data and First Algorithms

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: Where You Are, and How Computers Store Information
topics: A friendly diagnostic: your Land, school type, Klasse and what your Informatik class is doing now
How we work in English: the mentor's pace, the phrases for asking to slow down or repeat, and a German to English word list
Information and data: why a computer only stores numbers, and what a bit and a byte are
Binary numbers, counting in binary on your fingers and converting small numbers
Encoding text (ASCII and Unicode) and pictures (pixels and colours)
Starting an Informatik notebook with English and German terms side by side
projects: A secret message written in binary, decoded by a classmate in class
week_1_2.practice: Short binary and encoding puzzles of our own after each class

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Algorithms in Scratch: Sequence, Loops and Conditions
topics: What an algorithm is: precise, step by step, finished in finite time
Sequence, repetition and selection: the three building blocks
Events, sprites, costumes and coordinates in Scratch
Repeat loops and forever loops, and when each one fits
If and if-else with sensing blocks
Describing an algorithm out loud in English before building it
projects: A maze game where a sprite reacts to walls and keys
week_3_4.practice: Build-then-explain tasks: each Scratch program is described in three English sentences
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: a short quiz of our own on binary, encoding and Scratch control structures

month_2_variables_lists_structure_charts.title: Month 2: Variables, Lists, Structure Charts and Puzzle Thinking

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Variables, Lists and Messages in Scratch
topics: Variables for score, lives and timers, and changing them safely
Lists in Scratch: storing many values and looping through them
Broadcast messages so sprites can cooperate
Random numbers and simple simulations
Finding and fixing bugs by tracing the program step by step
Reading someone else's Scratch project and explaining what it does
projects: A quiz game that stores questions in a list and keeps score
week_5_6.practice: Debugging challenges: a broken project of ours to repair each week

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Structure Charts, Searching, Sorting and Puzzles
topics: Writing algorithms as Struktogramme (Nassi-Shneiderman structure charts) and flowcharts
Linear search, and why a sorted list allows a faster search
Sorting by hand: comparing and swapping, and counting the steps
Puzzle-style computational thinking of the kind the Informatik-Biber is known for (our own puzzles)
Breaking a big problem into smaller ones
Explaining why an algorithm is correct, in clear English
projects: A Scratch animation that sorts a row of numbered cards step by step
week_7_8.practice: Our own logic puzzles, solved and then explained aloud
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a Scratch task plus written questions on algorithms and data

phase_2_python_and_data.title: PHASE 2: From Blocks to Python, and Working with Data (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_python_and_data.description: The move from Scratch to text code in Python, a clear and widely used language, then real data and simple encryption.

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: From Blocks to Text Code
topics: Each Scratch block and its Python twin: loops, conditions and variables
Input, output and data types: numbers, text and true or false
If, elif and else, and comparison operators
Reading Python error messages calmly and fixing them
Writing comments that explain the code in English
Pacing: younger batches take more time here, older batches move on faster
projects: A number-guessing game in Python with hints and a guess counter
week_9_10.practice: Small daily Python tasks, each with one sentence of explanation

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Loops, Functions and Turtle Graphics
topics: For loops with range and while loops with a condition
Functions with parameters and return values
Turtle graphics: drawing shapes and patterns with loops
Nested loops and patterns
Testing a function with chosen inputs
Turning a structure chart into Python and back
projects: A turtle drawing program that builds a pattern from your own functions
week_11_12.practice: Trace tables for short programs, written in class and checked together
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a short Python program plus trace-table questions

month_4_data_and_encryption.title: Month 4: Lists, Text, Encryption and Data Tables

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Lists, Strings and the Caesar Cipher
topics: Python lists: adding, removing, searching and looping
Strings: characters, slicing and character codes
Encryption: the Caesar cipher and why it is easy to break
Frequency analysis: breaking a cipher by counting letters
Why modern encryption matters for messages and online banking
Explaining a cipher to a partner in English
projects: A Caesar cipher tool that encrypts, decrypts and cracks a message
week_13_14.practice: Our own cipher puzzles, solved first by hand and then in code

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Data Tables, Charts and Privacy
topics: Data in tables: rows, columns and records
Reading a CSV file in Python and calculating totals and averages
Simple charts from data and what a misleading chart looks like
Personal data and privacy, and why data protection rules exist
Collecting a small survey in class and analysing it
Presenting a finding in English in under two minutes
projects: A class survey analysed in Python with a short spoken presentation
week_15_16.practice: Data questions of our own on tables, averages and charts
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a Python task with lists and data plus written questions

phase_3_systems_networks_society.title: PHASE 3: Informatiksysteme, Networks, Automata, Society and AI (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_systems_networks_society.description: The remaining GI content areas, which Klasse 7 to 10 classes meet in many Länder, finished with a school-test style review and a final project.

month_5_systems_and_networks.title: Month 5: How Computers and Networks Work

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Inside a Computer
topics: The EVA-Prinzip: input, processing and output
Hardware and software, the processor, memory and storage
Logic gates AND, OR and NOT, and simple truth tables
How an operating system shares the computer between programs
Files, file types and sizes in kilobytes and megabytes
Describing a computer system in English with the right words
projects: A truth-table checker in Python for small logic circuits
week_17_18.practice: Labelling and explaining diagrams of computer systems, in English

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: The Internet, the Web and Staying Safe
topics: Networks, routers and packets: how a message crosses the internet
IP addresses, domain names and DNS
Clients, servers and HTTP, and what a browser actually does
A first web page in HTML with a heading, a list and a link
Passwords, phishing and two-factor sign-in
Network questions of the kind school tests ask, answered in full sentences
projects: A personal web page about a hobby, written in HTML
week_19_20.practice: Our own network scenarios to explain step by step
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: written questions on systems, networks and safety

month_6_automata_society_review.title: Month 6: Automata, AI, Society and Review

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Automata, Rules and Artificial Intelligence
topics: Sprachen und Automaten: a traffic light and a vending machine as state machines
Rules that decide whether a word or code is valid
How a simple AI learns from examples, and why the examples matter
Bias, mistakes and fairness in AI systems
Using AI tools honestly for schoolwork, and when not to use them
Informatik, Mensch und Gesellschaft: a class debate in English
projects: A state machine in Python for a traffic light, plus a one-page AI explainer
week_21_22.practice: Short debates and written answers on AI, privacy and society

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: School-Test Style Review and Final Project
topics: Review of the topics the pupil's own Klasse is testing this term
Mixed questions of our own written in the style of school Informatik tests
Planning a final project: idea, structure chart, code and testing
Building and testing the project in Scratch or Python
Presenting the project in English to the batch
A plan for the next school year's Informatik
projects: A final project of the pupil's choice, presented live in English
week_23_24.practice: A timed mixed review of our own questions
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: a programming task, written questions and a short spoken explanation

faqs.question: What is the Informatik Companion course?
faqs.answer: A live online course for pupils in Germany in Klasse 5 to 10 (roughly ages 10 to 16) that covers school Informatik: algorithms in Scratch and Python, information and data, computers and networks, automata, and informatics in society including AI. It runs for 24 weeks with 2 live classes a week, taught in English.

faqs.question: Are the classes in German or in English?
faqs.answer: English only. We never teach in German. The mentor matches the pupil's pace and accent: speaks clearly, slows down, repeats and rephrases, and checks understanding often. Many families see this as a plus, because the pupil gets Informatik help and spoken English practice in the same hour. Our notes put the German school term beside the English one so class links back to school.

faqs.question: My English is not perfect. Can I still join?
faqs.answer: Yes. The course is designed for pupils whose first language is not English. You can ask the mentor to slow down or repeat at any time, code itself uses mostly English words, and you explain your programs out loud in simple sentences that get easier every week. The free first class shows you whether the pace suits you.

faqs.question: Does the course match Informatik in my Land?
faqs.answer: It follows the common ground of all Länder: the five content areas of the GI recommended standards for Sekundarstufe I. Because Informatik differs a lot between Länder (for example compulsory in Klasse 5 and 6 in NRW, in Klasse 9 and 10 in Niedersachsen, four weekly hours over Klasse 7 to 10 in Hamburg and Schleswig-Holstein, per the GI Informatik-Monitor 2026/27), the mentor asks about your Land, school type and Klasse in the first class and weights the course toward what your class is doing.

faqs.question: My Land has no compulsory Informatik. Is this still useful?
faqs.answer: Yes. The GI Informatik-Monitor 2026/27 names six Länder with no Informatik compulsory for everyone: Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Hessen, Rheinland-Pfalz and Sachsen-Anhalt. Pupils there often meet Informatik as an elective, or later in the Oberstufe, and this course gives them the foundations early. Bremen plans a compulsory subject from 2027/28 and Rheinland-Pfalz from 2028/29.

faqs.question: Scratch or Python: which one will my child learn?
faqs.answer: Both, in that order. Younger pupils (around Klasse 5 to 7) spend longer in Scratch, so ideas such as loops and variables are clear before any text code. Older pupils (around Klasse 8 to 10) move faster into Python. Batches are grouped by Klasse so the pace fits.

faqs.question: Will you help with homework from school?
faqs.answer: We explain the ideas behind school tasks and practise with our own similar exercises, so the pupil can do the homework alone. We do not do the homework for the pupil.

faqs.question: When are the classes, given the time difference?
faqs.answer: Timing is flexible on weekdays or weekends: choose a batch, or choose 1-on-1 at your convenience. Our teachers work in India time, which is 4 hours 30 minutes ahead of Germany in winter and 3 hours 30 minutes ahead in summer, so German afternoon, early evening and weekend slots are realistic.

faqs.question: Is this the same as the Informatik-Biber?
faqs.answer: No. The Informatik-Biber is a free online quiz run by BWINF for grades 3 to 13, with the 2026 Biber weeks from 9 to 20 November 2026. Our puzzle-style lessons build the same kind of thinking, but we are not connected to BWINF. For competitions in depth there is our German Informatics Competitions course.

faqs.question: Is Modern Age Coders a recognised German school or provider?
faqs.answer: No. We are an independent online school with teachers in India. We are not a German school, we are not linked to any Land ministry or to the GI, and our certificate is not a German grade or qualification. It records what the pupil has learned with us.

faqs.question: What does a pupil need?
faqs.answer: A computer with a stable internet connection and a headset or earphones with a microphone. Scratch runs in the browser, and we help install Python in class.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first class is a free demo, so the pupil can meet the mentor, hear the pace and decide with no pressure.
